title: Security and compliance certifications and Trust Centers

opening.headline: The scope of certification and the shared responsibility model explain why just saying a vendor is certified is not enough.
body: At a meeting introducing an AI tool, it's easy for the vendor to respond with "We've got SOC 2" and the conversation end there. However, we need to check separately whether the certification includes the products and plans we will use, and where the responsibility of the certified party diverges from that of us.

In this class, we'll look at what resources a vendor's Trust Center collects, how to read certification tables by product, and how the shared responsibility model divides the work between the provider and the customer. At the end, we will solve a case where an accident occurred due to settings even though there was authentication.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what Trust Center and security/compliance documents are and how they are structured
In the shared responsibility model, the responsibility of the provider and the responsibility of the customer can be distinguished.

screens.title: Is one certificate enough?
screens.lead: This is a common scene during introduction review meetings. As you read, think about what questions your security team might ask next.

visual.alt: A scene at a conference table where a vendor holds out an authentication document and the security team holds up two question marks.
labels: Are the products and plans we plan to use in scope?
What is our responsibility after certification?

paragraphs: At the adoption review meeting, the vendor responded, “We got SOC 2.” This may sound reassuring, but security teams have two more questions to ask: Does the certification include the products and plans we will use, and what do we need to do apart from the certification?

Even if there is certification, if our settings are poor, the cause of the accident may be on our side. For example, if data is leaked from a workspace with all external sharing open, even if the provider's authentication is valid, the settings are set by the customer.
So there are two things to check. The scope of certification and our share. This lesson covers how to read both.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how we each reviewed our certificates.

screens.title: How do I review a vendor's certificate?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Do you just check the certification name, or do you also look at the scope and duration?
items.answer: The certification name is only a starting point. Even with the same vendor, certification may vary depending on the product and plan, and the report has an evaluation target and period. If we just check the name, we miss out on the product we're using.

items.prompt: Is there a list of things we need to do after getting certified?
items.answer: Without this list, it feels like certification solves everything. Items that need to be determined by the customer, such as permission design, sharing settings, and log collection, should be written down in advance to avoid any gaps after introduction.

items.prompt: Where do I get the certification documents and who keeps them?
items.answer: Consider whether the vendor has a disclosure channel, what procedures they use to receive sensitive documents, and whether they keep a review record of the documents they receive. The answer to this question is why you need Trust Center.

screens.outro: Now that we've got our ways out of the way, let's take a look at what's actually in the Trust Center.

screens.title: What's gathered at the Trust Center?
screens.lead: Selecting an item expands the types of materials the Anthropic Trust Center has collected in that area. Try to identify where to find the document.

visual.alt: Screen diagram showing the configuration of the Trust Center first screen.

items.title: Request access: request access
items.body: The Trust Center is an outlet for disclosing and requesting compliance documents. Sensitive documents can be viewed by clicking the "request access" button at the top of the page and filling out the request form. Once you gain this access, you can also ask questions about documents with the Trust Center AI feature.

items.title: Resources: Certificates and Reports
items.body: Resources include SOC 2 Report and SOC 3 Report, SOC 2 Bridge Letter, ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 Certificates, and ISO Declaration of Applicability. HIPAA reports and implementation guides, NIST 800-171 assurances, and FedRAMP certification packages are also located in the same location. The bridge letter is a document that bridges the period between the report's assessment period and the present and is therefore read in conjunction with the report.

items.title: Resources: Policies, white papers, model documents
items.body: Additional features include a Code of Conduct, Security Best Practices and Cryptographic Key Design White Paper, Security Advisories, Model Document Forms, Training Data Summary, Data Processing Annex (DPA), Penetration Test Report, and Accessibility Conformance Report. Depending on the purpose of your review, you will need different documents, so we recommend skimming through the list first.

items.title: Subprocessors and updates
items.body: The Subprocessors area lists external providers that handle data, such as cloud infrastructure or traffic routing. When the list is updated, news will be posted in the update area. This list serves as a basis for explaining where your data goes.

items.title: Similar documents from other providers
items.body: Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise documentation also provides a list of supported certifications and security control tables all in one place. Controls such as Data Residency (DRZ), Customer Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), VPC Service Controls, and Access Transparency are tabulated. Although the names of each provider are different, the structure of disclosing certification and control in documents is the same.

screens.outro: Now that we know where the document is, let's move on to reading the all-important authentication table.

screens.title: Read the certification table: Scope by product
screens.lead: The table below is a reorganized excerpt from the Trust Center's certification table. Compare how the columns are different for each product even if it is a certification with the same name.

data.caption: Examples of certification marks by product
rows: Claude in Microsoft Foundry, hosted on Azure
data.notes: N/A means the product is not within the scope of that certification, and Partner-Managed means it is an area managed by the partner. In-Process is a sign that something is in progress. A footnote below the table explains that the Bedrock and Vertex AI items apply only to the model itself and the containers provided by Anthropic to its partners. SOC 2 is a report in which an independent auditor evaluates a service organization's controls, and Type 2 even evaluates whether the controls were actually operated over a certain period of time. Therefore, what you need to read in the table is not the name of the certification, but the point where the line for the product you want to use and the column for the certification you need meet. If the field is empty or marked as Partner Managed, you will need to request a report or check your partner documentation separately.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read scope, let's look at the shared responsibility model for responsibilities that remain outside of certification.

screens.title: Commentary: Workspace leaked even though there is authentication
screens.lead: The instructor walks through a case and narrows down where responsibility lay. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Illustration of a shared responsibility model in which the responsibility area of the provider and the area of responsibility of the customer are divided up and down.
labels: security of the cloud: provider responsibility
security in the cloud: customer responsibility
Boundaries move depending on service type

steps.title: Cases and Questions
steps.body: In a company that introduced certified AI tools, internal data was leaked through a workspace that had allowed all external sharing. The question is, “Why was there a leak if the vendor was certified?” Let's narrow down where the blame lay, from the inside out.

steps.title: AWS classification: of and in
steps.body: AWS explains that security and compliance are split between providers and customers. The provider protects the hardware, software, network, and facilities that run the service, and calls this “security of the cloud.” Customers are responsible for security in the cloud, that is, data and settings.

steps.title: Service type changes share
steps.body: The customer's portion varies depending on which service is selected. For example, Amazon EC2 is classified as IaaS, so customers are responsible for updating the guest OS, updating security patches, installing application software, and even setting up security group firewalls. The more managed services are used, the thicker the layer the provider is responsible for.

steps.title: Check the infrastructure and platform layers
steps.body: Moving to AI services, the provider's role is in the area of infrastructure and platform control, as well as certification. In this case, there was no indication that the infrastructure or platform had been compromised. Certification is still valid for this floor.

steps.title: Find the cause in the settings layer
steps.body: The leakage route was user permissions and sharing settings. Allowing all external sharing is a configuration decision made by the customer. This corresponds to what AWS calls “data and access settings” that are up to the customer.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Certification is proof of how the provider maintains its share, and is not a guarantee that the customer's settings will be replaced. So the adoption review should have “a list of settings that we need to set,” along with verification of certification.

screens.outro: Let's summarize the divisions identified in the case in table form.

screens.title: Commentary: Turning review results into a list of responsibilities
screens.lead: Alternate between the two options to compare who is responsible for the same items. At the end, the instructor organizes what will be left in the review document.

states.label: What the provider shows
states.body: It is the responsibility of the provider to control the data center and infrastructure, secure platform-level security controls, and evaluate certification reports and renewal documents. The provider discloses this evidence through a channel such as the Trust Center, and sensitive documents go through a request process. Guidance on data processing, retention, and deletion is also available in the Security and Compliance collection of product help. Subprocessor lists and data processing annexes also fall into this category. In summary, the provider's job is to "prove and disclose," and the customer's job is to "decide and operate based on it." Switch between the two views to see which function items are classified into which one. It is safer to write down items with ambiguous classification as the customer's responsibility until a person in charge is identified.

states.label: What the customer must leave behind
states.body: The customer decides how to design roles and permissions, how far to open external sharing and connectors, how to collect and store logs, and how to organize accounts of employees who have left the company. It is also the customer's responsibility to educate users about the company's policies. These items will not be filled in no matter how much you read the certification report. In your review results document, it is a good idea to include a separate “Customer Responsibilities” section alongside the scope of certification and note who is responsible and when.

screens.outro: Now, I will organize the contents so far into one standard.

screens.title: Authentication is the starting point and configuration is an ongoing responsibility
screens.lead: Let's group the contents of this class into one judgment standard. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: When reviewing vendor certification, we look at three things in order: First, how are the products and plans we will use indicated in the certification table? Second, what scope and period did the report assess? Third, what should we do in areas not covered by the report?

The Trust Center is a place where the information needed for this verification is gathered in one place. There are certificates and reports, a list of subprocessors, frequently asked questions, and access requests for sensitive documents. Documents received will be recorded as a review and kept with the scope of certification.

The shared responsibility model is a framework for interpreting these results. The provider is responsible for the service base and its authentication, and the customer is responsible for the data, permissions and settings on it. Since the customer's share varies depending on which service is used, this distinction must be re-checked when changing AI tools.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The fact that there is certification answers the question on the provider side. Customer questions still need to be answered by us. If you record the two questions separately, you can use them as a basis for audits or reviews.

checks.intro: We just looked at reading the authentication table. Pick the first thing to check in the meeting scene. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: At the introduction review meeting, the vendor responded, ‘We have received SOC 2.’ What should the security team check first?
options: Are the products and plans we plan to use within the scope of the report?
If we know that we have been certified, will we be exempt from setting up the responsibility?
What is the cover design and publishing department for the SOC 2 report?
If there is at least one authentication name, there is no need to check other authentications.
checks.correctFeedback: It is correct to consider the scope of application rather than the name of the certification.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This selection is not a question confirming the scope of the certification.
checks.explain: The certification table varies depending on the product and plan. Even with the same Claude, the HIPAA field for the Team plan may be N/A, so we need to read whether the product we are going to use is in scope.

wrong.1: Even with certification, setup responsibility remains with the customer.
wrong.2: This is a formal matter and has nothing to do with the scope of application of the certification.
wrong.3: The required certifications vary from requirement to requirement and cannot be replaced by a single name.

checks.intro: We have presented an example of the shared responsibility model. Match the terms with their meanings. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Pair the concepts of the Shared Responsibility Model and Certification Document with explanations.
right: A report in which an independent auditor evaluates the effectiveness of control operations over a certain period of time
Areas where the customer is responsible, such as data, access rights and settings
A window to disclose compliance documents and request access to sensitive documents
Areas for which the provider is responsible for the security of the infrastructure itself
checks.correctFeedback: We accurately linked the provider's share, the customer's share, and the nature of the supporting documents.
checks.incorrectFeedback: A few connections are out of alignment. Let's start by dividing it again, which side is the infrastructure and which side is the settings above it.
checks.explain: The provider is responsible for the infrastructure and authentication, and the customer is responsible for the data, permissions, and settings. Certification reports and Trust Center are means of verifying the provider's evidence.

glossary.def: This is where vendors disclose their certifications, reports, subprocessors, and frequently asked questions. Sensitive documents are viewed after requesting access.
A reporting framework in which an independent auditor evaluates a service organization's security controls. Type 2 also evaluates operational effectiveness over a certain period of time.

The distinction is that the provider is responsible for service-based security, and the customer is responsible for the data, permissions, and settings. The customer's share varies depending on the service used.
A collection of vendor-provided evidence, such as certificates, audit reports, security questionnaire responses, white papers, and policy documents. You should keep a record of your review.

misconceptions.myth: Since the vendor is certified, we are compliant.
misconceptions.fact: Certification shows that the provider has controls in place in its area. Customer areas such as user permissions, sharing settings, and log collection are the customer's responsibility, independent of authentication.

misconceptions.myth: All products and plans with the same certification name are included.
misconceptions.fact: Certification tables display differently depending on the product and plan. Even within the same vendor, some fields are divided into Certified, some are N/A, and some are Partner Management.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Certification demonstrates the responsibility of the provider, while settings are the responsibility of the customer.
Certification only makes sense if you read the scope for each product and plan.
Access to sensitive documents from the Trust Center is requested and received, and a review record is kept.
In a shared responsibility model, the customer's share depends on the type of service.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: To what extent does our organization have direct responsibility, separate from certification? Think about whether there are any permissions, sharing, or logs for which the person in charge has not yet been determined.
